What are the three criteria of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6–59 months? (Any one is enough.)
A mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) below 11.5 cm, a weight-for-height below −3 standard deviations, or bilateral pitting oedema.
What is the MUAC range of moderate acute malnutrition (MAM)?
From 11.5 cm to below 12.5 cm; the weight-for-height is between −3 and −2 standard deviations.
What are the two clinical forms of SAM?
SAM without oedema (marasmus) and SAM with oedema (kwashiorkor). Oedema together with severe wasting is the most severe form.
A child has a low weight-for-age but a normal weight-for-height. Is the child wasted?
No. This is underweight, not wasting; wasting is a low weight-for-height.
A child has bilateral pitting oedema and a normal MUAC. What is the diagnosis?
SAM with oedema (oedematous malnutrition), whatever the weight or MUAC.
What is the dietary cause of SAM without oedema?
A deficiency of total energy (calories and protein): starvation.
At what age does SAM without oedema usually occur?
What are the behaviour and appetite of a child with SAM without oedema?
The child is alert, irritable and hungry.
Which is the last site to lose fat in SAM without oedema?
The buccal pad of fat in the cheeks; its loss gives the "old man" face.
What is the dietary cause of SAM with oedema?
Protein deficiency with fairly adequate calories (a starchy diet), often triggered by infection.
At what age does SAM with oedema usually occur?
Which feature is essential for the diagnosis of SAM with oedema (kwashiorkor)?
What are the constant features of SAM with oedema?
Oedema, growth failure, mental changes (apathy), and muscle wasting with preserved fat.
Alternating pale and dark bands along the hair, reflecting periods of poor and better nutrition.
Dark patches of skin that peel off and leave raw skin, on the legs, buttocks and napkin area.
What causes the hepatomegaly of SAM with oedema?
Fatty infiltration of the liver: apolipoprotein is low, so fat cannot leave the liver.
What is the most characteristic laboratory finding in SAM with oedema?
Which has the worse prognosis: SAM without oedema or SAM with oedema?
SAM with oedema, because infections and electrolyte problems are more common.
Which grade of oedema reaches the face, and what is done?
Grade +++ (severe, generalised oedema). The child is admitted.
What is the commonest cause of death in SAM?
How is hypoglycaemia defined in SAM?
A blood glucose below 3 mmol/L (54 mg/dL).
How is hypothermia defined in SAM?
An axillary temperature below 35 °C (rectal temperature below 35.5 °C).
What are the reliable signs of dehydration in SAM?
A history of watery diarrhoea, recently sunken eyes, a weak radial pulse and little urine.
Feeding a starved child too fast causes low phosphate, potassium and magnesium, which can lead to heart failure.
What are the indications to admit a child with SAM?
A medical complication, a failed appetite test, oedema grade +++, oedema with severe wasting, or an infant under 6 months who is not feeding well.
How is the appetite test done?
The child is offered the test amount of ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) for his weight. If he eats it within 30 minutes he passes and is treated in the outpatient therapeutic programme (OTP).
How is hypoglycaemia treated in a conscious child with SAM?
50 ml of 10% glucose (or sugar water) by mouth or nasogastric tube, followed by F-75.
How is hypoglycaemia treated in an unconscious child with SAM?
10% glucose 5 ml/kg intravenously, then 50 ml by nasogastric tube.
How is a child with SAM rewarmed?
Skin-to-skin (kangaroo) contact with the mother, covering the head, a warm room and immediate feeding. Hot-water bottles are not used.
Which fluid is used to rehydrate a child with SAM who is not in shock, and how?
ReSoMal: 5 ml/kg every 30 minutes for 2 hours, then 5–10 ml/kg per hour for 4–10 hours.
What are the sodium and potassium contents of ReSoMal?
Sodium 45 and potassium 40 mmol/L (standard ORS: sodium 75 and potassium 20 mmol/L).
What is the only indication for intravenous fluid in SAM?
How is severe anaemia (haemoglobin below 4 g/dL) treated in SAM?
Packed cells or whole blood 10 ml/kg over 3 hours.
Are diuretics used for the oedema of SAM?
Which antibiotic is given in SAM without complications?
Which antibiotics are given in complicated SAM?
Ampicillin 50 mg/kg 6-hourly for 2 days, then amoxicillin, together with gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg daily for 7 days.
When is iron started in SAM?
In the rehabilitation phase (week 2), when the child is gaining weight.
When is high-dose vitamin A given in SAM, and what is the dose over 12 months of age?
Only with eye signs or measles, because the therapeutic feeds already contain vitamin A: 200 000 IU on days 1, 2 and 14.
What are the energy and protein contents of F-75?
75 kcal and 0.9 g of protein per 100 ml.
How is F-75 given on days 1–2?
11 ml/kg every 2 hours (12 feeds a day), which is 130 ml/kg/day.
When is F-75 changed to F-100 or RUTF?
When the appetite returns and the oedema is reducing.
What is the target weight gain in the rehabilitation phase?
During transition to F-100, the pulse rises by 25/min and the breathing by 5/min. What should be done?
These are warning signs of heart failure: the feed volume is reduced.

What is the main advantage of RUTF at home?
It needs no water or cooking, so it does not become contaminated.
What are the cure criteria for SAM?
A MUAC of 12.5 cm or more and/or a weight-for-height of −2 standard deviations or more (the same measure as at admission), with no oedema, on 2 consecutive visits.
How is moderate acute malnutrition treated?
In a targeted supplementary feeding programme, with ready-to-use supplementary food (RUSF) or corn-soya blend, and visits every 2 weeks.
What is the first sign of recovery in SAM?
The return of appetite and smiling, at days 3–4.
